content: The United States Public Health Service (PHS) is composed of all agency divisions within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Commissioned Corps. The Assistant Secretary for Health (ASH) oversees both the PHS and the United States Public Health Service Commissioned Corps. The PHS is an elite team of over 6,000 highly trained and qualified public health professionals who are committed to implementing the nation’s public health promotion and disease prevention programs while advancing public health science. These professionals, driven by a passion for public service, work on the frontlines of the nation’s efforts to combat disease and poor health conditions. As one of the seven uniformed services of the United States, the Commissioned Corps provides critical public health leadership and service roles within federal government agencies and programs. Officers in the Corps represent a wide range of professions, including environmental and occupational health, medicine, nursing, dentistry, pharmacy, psychology, social work, hospital administration, health record administration, dietetics, engineering, science, veterinary medicine, and other health-related fields. The mission of the PHS Commissioned Corps is to protect, promote, and advance the health and safety of the United States. This mission is achieved through rapid and effective responses to public health needs, leadership and excellence in public health practices, and the advancement of public health science. The Commissioned Corps is an integral part of the world’s largest public health program, offering professional opportunities in areas such as occupational health and safety, environmental health, disease control and prevention, biomedical research, regulation of food, drugs, and medical devices, mental health and substance abuse, healthcare delivery, and international health. Officers in the Corps have opportunities for mobility across government agencies and career advancement in diverse work settings. They gain varied experiences and are encouraged to expand their knowledge and grow professionally to address the challenges of improving public health effectively. Tuition and long-term training opportunities may also be available. Although the Commissioned Corps is a uniformed service, it is not part of the armed forces. Officers are compensated according to military pay scales, are eligible for military healthcare (TRICARE) for themselves and their dependents, and are covered under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act of 2003. Additional information about employment opportunities can be found on the Commissioned Corps website. The origins of the Public Health Service date back to 1798, with the passage of an act providing care and relief for sick and injured merchant seamen. The earliest marine hospitals were established along the East Coast, with the first facility located in Boston. Over time, hospitals were also established along inland waterways, the Great Lakes, and the Gulf of Mexico and Pacific Coasts. In 1871, the position of Supervising Surgeon (later Surgeon General) was created to administer the Service, with John Maynard Woodworth appointed as the first incumbent. Woodworth reformed the system by adopting a military model for the medical staff, instituting examinations for applicants, and requiring physicians to wear uniforms. He created a cadre of mobile, career service physicians who could be assigned as needed to various marine hospitals. The uniformed services component of the Marine Hospital Service was formalized as the Public Health Service Commissioned Corps through legislation enacted in 1889. Initially open only to physicians, the Corps expanded throughout the 20th century to include dentists, sanitary engineers, pharmacists, nurses, sanitarians, scientists, and other health professionals. The scope of activities of the Marine Hospital Service also expanded beyond the care of merchant seamen, beginning with the control of infectious diseases. The National Quarantine Act of 1878 transferred quarantine authority from the states to the Marine Hospital Service, and over the next 50 years, the Service increasingly assumed quarantine functions from state authorities. As immigration surged in the late 19th century, the federal government took over the processing of immigrants from the states, starting in 1891. The Marine Hospital Service was tasked with the medical inspection of arriving immigrants at sites such as Ellis Island in New York. Commissioned officers played a significant role in preventing the entry of diseases into the country. Due to the expanding responsibilities of the Service, its name was changed in 1902 to the Public Health and Marine Hospital Service, and again in 1912 to the Public Health Service. The Service continued to broaden its public health activities as the nation entered the 20th century, with the Commissioned Corps leading the way. Throughout the century, PHS commissioned officers served the country by controlling the spread of contagious diseases such as smallpox and yellow fever, conducting critical biomedical research, regulating the food and drug supply, providing healthcare to underserved populations, offering medical assistance after disasters, and in many other capacities. Today, the mission of the PHS Commissioned Corps is Protecting, promoting, and advancing the health and safety of the Nation. Members of the Public Health Service Commissioned Corps wear uniforms similar to those of the United States Navy, with distinctive PHS Corps devices and rank insignia identical to those of Naval officers. Two sets of rank titles are used: standard Navy rank titles and titles that reflect the officer’s specialty. For example, an officer at the grade of O-5/Commander is referred to as a Senior Surgeon, while an officer at the grade of O-3/Lieutenant is called a Senior Assistant. Since 1999, the Commissioned Corps emergency response teams have been managed by the Office of the Surgeon General. These teams are trained and equipped to respond to public health crises and national emergencies, including natural disasters, disease outbreaks, and terrorist attacks. The teams are multidisciplinary and capable of responding to both domestic and international humanitarian missions.
